passages.original: χάρις ὥσπερ Ἶρις τεταμένη καὶ τὴν πόλιν ὥσπερ λύραν ἁρμοττομένη σύμφωνον αὑτῇ τε καὶ τοῖς ἔξω κόσμοις, καὶ ἡ διὰ πάντων ὥσπερ τοῦ παρʼ Ὁμήρῳ χαλκοῦ μέχρι οὐρανοῦ διηνεκὴς αἴγλη, τῷ ταῦτα ἐφικτὰ διηγήσασθαι; οὐχ οὕτως οὔτε ὁ Μέλης καλλίπαις οὔτε τις εἰς λόγους εὐτυχής. καὶ μὴν μόνη μὲν πόλεων ἱστορίας, οὐκ ἀκοῆς δεῖται, μόνη δὲ οὐχ ἱστορίας μᾶλλον ἢ διαίτης συνεχοῦς καὶ ὁμιλίας, ὅστις αὐτὴν μέλλει καλῶς θεάσεσθαι καὶ τοὺς μισθοὺς τῶν ἐπαίνων αὐτόθεν κομιεῖσθαι.
passages.english: …grace stretched out like Iris [the rainbow], tuning the city like a lyre to be in harmony both with itself and with the adornments outside it, and the radiance running unbroken through everything up to heaven, like the bronze in Homer, who could describe these things adequately? Not so [fortunate] is either the Meles, with its fair offspring, or anyone fortunate in eloquence. And indeed, alone among cities it requires being seen, not being heard about; and alone it requires not so much seeing as continual residence and familiarity, for anyone who means to view it properly and to receive on the spot the rewards of his praises.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject and main construction of the opening clauses lie in preceding text not supplied. 'Iris' is taken as the rainbow, personified. The 'bronze in Homer' alludes to the Homeric gleam of bronze reaching to heaven. The Meles is the river of Smyrna, associated with Homer; 'fair-childed' (καλλίπαις) probably alludes to Homer as its son, so the sentence seems to mean that not even Homer could do justice to the city. The sentence 'οὐχ οὕτως... εὐτυχής' is elliptical and the reading 'not so [fortunate]' is uncertain. 'Being seen' and 'seeing' render ἱστορία in its sense of visual inquiry or autopsy.
